summary: The deck explains how ideas for frugal innovation emerge, linking the concept to related frameworks such as reverse innovation, BOP innovation, Gandhian innovation, grassroots innovation, and inclusive innovation. It uses case studies including Jaipur Foot, LifeStraw, Kenyan beehive fences, Ethiopian enset processing, rural Indian biomass cookstoves, and Indian e-rickshaws to show both successful principles and common failures around human-centered design, co-creation, sustainability, adoption, and regulation.

content: How to Get Ideas for Frugal Innovation
“frugal”, drawn from the Latin word- frugalis, meaning "useful" or "thrifty"
Innovation starts in developing countries → moves to developed countries
Innovation for Bottom of Pyramid (low-income population), Affordable products for large poor population
Affordable excellence High quality + low cost “More from less for more people”
Innovation driven by understanding people’s problems deeply
Innovations that happen quietly without attention, Often in informal or rural sectors
Innovation that includes all sections of society, especially marginalized groups
Innovation from common people (not big companies), local solutions to local problems
All these concepts are related, but only some directly represent frugal innovation, while others focus on different aspects like market, users, or innovation process.
Artificial legs were very expensive Idea
Design a low-cost prosthetic for poor patients
Designed for Indian lifestyle (walking barefoot, sitting cross-legged)
Costs much lower than imported prosthetics
Dr. P. K. Sethi  and Ram Chandra Sharma saw:
A poor amputee struggling to walk
How Do Frugal Innovation Ideas Actually Come?
Start from Constraints (Not Resources):  Look at problems caused by lack of money, materials, or access;  “Do more with less” mindset
Focus on Real Problems (Bottom of Pyramid): Identify needs of rural users, low-income groups; Solve basic essential needs, not luxury features
Remove Non-Essential Features: Ask: What can be simplified or eliminated?  Simplicity = affordability
Use Collective Intelligence (Brainstorming): Generate ideas through team discussions and group brainstorming
Collaborate & Crowdsource Ideas: Work with Researchers, Startups, External partners
Think Human-Centered (Not Technology Centered): Focus on people’s needs, Practical usability
Identify Existing Gaps in Literature: Neglected sectors, Technology paradox (Specifically for you)
Unsafe drinking water in many countries

The International Centre for Frugal Innovation (ICFI)  is an academic research center within the strategic alliance between Leiden University, TU Delft and Erasmus University that focuses on accessible frugal innovation products, services, strategies and technologies.
Focusing on the research domains Health, Energy, Water and Agro-Food.
Farmers in Kenya face crop destruction by elephants
Traditional solutions (fences, fire) were costly or ineffective
When elephants touch the fence → bees get disturbed → elephants run away
Elephants avoided farms up to ~80–86% of the time
Beehive fences only work if bees are present
But bees are decreasing due to:
It does NOT solve the real problem
Why It is Still Good (Social Benefit)
Helps poor farmers who cannot afford expensive fencing
What is Needed for Real Sustainability
Summary : Good short-term solution, but long-term success needs deeper environmental changes.
Bees versus Elephants: a Battle that benefits Kenyan Agriculture
Ethiopia faces food insecurity due to:
Farmers need a reliable food source
Enset (a local crop) is strong and climate-resistant
Simple manual machines to process enset faster
Women do most of the farming work
But they don’t own land and take decisions
Women were not included in research, engineering, product design, decision making.
Women became users of the technology
Local women were NOT involved in design
Good frugal innovation should be developed with the community, not only for the community.
Poor farmers may not afford access
If people are not involved in creating the solution, they may not fully benefit from it.
Women of the Tree against Hunger
In rural India, people cook using traditional chulhas (wood, dung, crop waste)
Serious health problems (especially for women & children)
Features: Less smoke, More efficient, Low-cost
Company made a low-cost, improved cooking stove.
Problem 1: Focused only on product, not people
But did not ask: Will people actually use it long-term?
Poor families care about cost, daily benefit
If money-saving is not clear, they won’t switch
Only ~9% people continued using the stove
A good product failed because it ignored people’s habits, needs, and long-term realities.
Standards and Frugal innovation: Example of e-rickshaws in India
E-rickshaws were not invented in big labs
Built using: available parts, simple design
Innovation can start from people, not labs
But to scale safely, rules are necessary
Summary: E-rickshaws show that frugal innovation can grow rapidly without rules, but long-term success requires balancing innovation with safety standards.
No rules, No safety standards, No proper regulation
